title: KV cache shelf allocator, compact rings, and staged reclamation (design sketch)
content:
Purpose and scope:
This is a working sketch for an alternative in-memory KV cache allocator aimed at reducing fragmentation and improving tail-latency predictability for the serving runtime. It combines three ideas we haven't fully explored in the repo: shelf-style fixed slab shelves for hot small objects, compact ring allocators for medium objects, and a staged reclamation/compaction pipeline for large objects and sparse pages. This doc focuses on the allocator/layout semantics, eviction heuristics that interact well with the layout, and operational observability hooks.

Goals (ranked):
- Limit memory fragmentation over long-lived workloads (multi-day) without heavy stop-the-world compaction.
- Keep hot-path allocations/deallocations lock-light and cache-friendly.
- Make eviction decisions cheaper and less likely to cause head-of-line blocking.
- Provide incremental compaction that can be throttled by SLOs (latency/cpu/io).
- Be NUMA-aware and play well with hugepages and kernel-level hints (MADV_DONTNEED/MADV_FREE).

High-level idea summary:
1) Shelf allocator for hot, small KV entries (<= 512B).
   - Allocate a set of fixed-size "shelves" (small contiguous buffers) per shard/arena. Each shelf is dedicated to a size class (32B, 64B, 128B, 256B, 512B).
   - Shelves are monotonic bump allocators with a tiny free-list for recently freed slots to reuse within the shelf.
   - Hotness tracking is per-entry (compact LRU-ish tag) + per-shelf hit counter. Very hot shelves get pinned and replicated read-only across worker threads (read copies) for read-heavy workloads.

2) Compact ring allocators for medium objects (512B..64KB).
   - Each size class has a circular allocation region (a ring) that advances with allocations. Deallocation marks a slot as tombstone. The ring is periodically scanned by a background cleaner that compacts live entries toward the head and reclaims the tail continuously (amortized compaction).
   - Rings are lock-stripable by cacheline to allow concurrent alloc/unalloc; reclamation is done with CAS-based handoff to avoid global locks.

3) Large objects (>64KB) go to a separate large-pool per-NUMA node with an explicit free-list and async compaction pass that tries to coalesce adjacent free ranges.

Staged reclamation pipeline (background tasks):
- Stage 0: lightweight tombstone sweeper. Runs frequently, clears per-thread free-lists into the shard free pool. Keeps hot-path cheap.
- Stage 1: ring compaction pass. Incremental windowed compaction: pick a window size W pages and move live entries into a destination buffer and update indirections. Throttled by CPU and I/O budget.
- Stage 2: page-level defrag & hugepage rebinding. Runs less frequently, attempts to coalesce mostly-empty pages into contiguous ranges and madvise freed ranges to the kernel.

Eviction heuristics that fit the layout:
- Hybrid cost metric: score = alpha * recency_score + beta * size_penalty + gamma * shelf_pressure + delta * affinity_penalty
  - recency_score: small decaying counter (exponentially decayed hits) stored in the header; avoids full LRU lists.
  - size_penalty: larger objects cheaper to evict per-byte when under memory pressure (to free more capacity quickly).
  - shelf_pressure: if a shelf is near capacity, entries in that shelf get a small additional pressure multiplier so small-object-heavy workloads don't starve medium-object eviction.
  - affinity_penalty: penalize evicting entries that are currently pinned by an in-flight request or part of a cached prefix chain.
- Eviction flow: background eviction daemon computes candidate buckets by scanning per-shard pressure indicators (cheap counters), then picks victims using the hybrid score. For rings, eviction is often implemented as advancing the tail pointer and letting compaction pick live entries to keep. For shelves, we evict entire blocks when shelf occupancy crosses a high-water mark (fast bulk eviction).

Memory pools and NUMA:
- Each NUMA node has independent arenas: shelf arenas, ring arenas (by size class), large object pool. Allocation tries local node first, then remote if allowed by policy.
- Prefer binding compact rings to hugepages so compaction can operate on page-aligned memory and madvise ranges cheaply. For small-shelf arenas we avoid hugepages to keep per-slot overhead tiny.

Fragmentation mitigation techniques (summary):
- Size classes tuned to workload histogram. We need an offline profiler that suggests splits by looking at real token/prefix distributions.
- Shelf reclamation + bulk-evict reduces interleaving of small and large allocations.
- Incremental compaction windows reduce peak CPU while gradually reducing fragmentation.
- Opportunistic page shuffling during low-load windows to improve contiguity for hugepages.

Observability and metrics (must have):
- Per-shard: free-bytes, used-bytes, fragmentation-estimate (bytes-lost-to-internal-fragmentation), shelf-occupancy-by-class, ring-head-tail-gap, compaction-progress, compaction-throughput (MB/s).
- Per-request tracing: allocation latency histogram, hits that required relocation during compaction, eviction-triggered fetches.
- Heatmap: a time-series matrix of hotness vs size class to feed Optimize suggestions.

Open implementation notes and questions (brain dump):
- Indirections: moving live entries during ring compaction requires updating pointers used by in-flight requests. We need a light-weight indirection table per-shard (atomic pointer table) so moves can install new locations and a generation counter to avoid ABA hazards. Is the cost of an indirection acceptable on high-qps routes?
- Shelves with tiny freelists: fragmentation internal to a shelf is small but external fragmentation (shelves sitting partially full) can accumulate. Should we implement shelf-sharing across shards? That increases locking complexity.
- Hugepages: if rings are backed by hugepages we get big wins for compaction/IO, but allocation granularity becomes coarse for medium objects. Potential hybrid: per-ring suballocation of hugepages but still allow fallback to normal pages.
- Background compaction throttle: expose a global and per-tenant throttle so enterprise customers can set compaction to lower priority during peak hours.
- Eviction fairness: long-tail queries might touch large entries. We should cap eviction preference for tiny objects so that a sequence of tiny evictions doesn't thrash for large items required by a single important request.

Prototype plan (next steps):
1) Implement the shelf allocator (single-shard) and microbench with synthetic small-object workloads including churn. Measure internal fragmentation and lock contention. (2 wk)
2) Implement compact ring prototype with a small background compactor and CAS-based head/tail. Test with a mixed workload (50% small, 40% medium, 10% large). (3 wk)
3) Add NUMA arenas + hugepage option and measure compaction throughput and tail latency impact. (2 wk)
4) Integrate hybrid eviction scoring and basic observability hooks. Run long-duration (72h) soak tests to observe fragmentation trends. (3 wk)

Unresolved questions to discuss in follow-up meeting:
- Should indirection be global per-shard or per-key? tradeoffs?
- How aggressive should shelf bulk eviction be when under memory pressure versus letting compaction handle it slowly?
- Operational surface: what knobs are safe to expose to customers vs internal defaults?

References / previous work:
- Related internal notes: kv-cache-frag-observability-playbook (confluence link above).
- External inspiration: Facebook Folly's Quarters alloc strategy, jemalloc arenas ideas, and Google Bigtable memtable compaction heuristics.

Notes to self:
- Keep the initial prototype single-threaded for correctness, then stress with the SRE harness.
- Add a synthetic workload generator that writes key-size distributions we see in hosted API telemetry.

Status: draft -> want to sync with Priya and Diego next Thurs to align on indirection approach and compaction safety model.
